walkthroughs.body_html: Plastics are synthetic polymers made mostly from fossil fuel feedstocks. Common types include PET (bottles), HDPE (milk jugs), LDPE (bags), PP (caps), PS (foam) and PVC (pipes). Plastic does not biodegrade in nature; it breaks into smaller pieces over decades or centuries. Global production has grown from 2 Mt in 1950 to around 400 Mt per year today.

Microplastics are pieces under 5 mm. Primary microplastics include nurdles (raw pellets), microbeads (banned in many cosmetics) and synthetic clothing fibres shed in washing. Secondary microplastics form as larger items break down. They are now found in tap water, table salt, Arctic snow and human blood, with unknown long-term health effects.

Ocean currents form five major gyres. The Great Pacific Garbage Patch is roughly three times the size of France, made of around 80,000 tonnes of plastic floating between Hawaii and California. It is not a solid island but a soup of fragments. Sunlight, waves and salt eventually break the plastic into smaller pieces that wildlife mistakes for food.
